title: Cab's letter about the Porgy and Bess pit band and Smallens's answer
summary: After six months with Hines, a letter from Cab (playing Sportin' Life) asked him to join the Ziegfeld pit band and Cab wanted eight black musicians; conductor Smallens said colour did not matter if they could read.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: How long were you with it?

Oh, I guess I stayed in there, oh, about six months, because the next year -- see, I stayed in there, say, from about April. Maybe a little longer than that. April to -- I think it was around April I went in there. From April to about January or February, when "Porgy and Bess" was getting ready to open up, because Cab had wrote me a letter when we was in California at the Oasis, asking me. Or another place we played with Earl called -- at Bush and Powell, The Hangover. It was Doc Dougherty's place. We played out there. And that's before he went out and become a house band there. Two or three years later he went back and stayed there. But we -- Cab had wrote me he was doing Sportin' Life. He wrote me a letter asking me would I be interested in playing in the pit band for "Porgy and Bess", at the Ziegfeld Theater, when the show opens up there. So I wrote him back and told him yes, you know. It was a challenge, like I told you at the beginning. I was taught to read, you know, pretty good. So I said yes. So he told me, "Well, I'm trying to get about eight men." He said they've got about 40 pieces, they're going to use about 40 pieces in the pit band, "and I'm trying to get at least eight blacks in there." So I went to Smallens already who was conducting the show, and I asked him did he object to having black musicians in the band.
